entities.summary:
Chabrias, an Athenian general of the 4th century BCE, stands as a pivotal figure in the resurgence of Athenian military power following the Peloponnesian War. Born around 500 BCE in Athens, his career spanned the tumultuous decades when Athens sought to reclaim its influence amidst the shifting hegemonies of Sparta and Thebes, ultimately dying in 356 BCE. He is celebrated for his innovative military tactics, particularly his defensive 'Chabrias' maneuver, and for his crucial role in re-establishing Athens as a dominant naval force in the Aegean Sea, thereby shaping the geopolitical landscape of the Classical Greek world.

His most celebrated achievement came in 376 BCE at the Battle of Naxos, where he decisively defeated the Spartan fleet, marking a turning point in Athenian naval history and effectively ending Spartan maritime supremacy. Earlier, in 378 BCE, during a campaign against Agesilaus II in Boeotia, Chabrias introduced a revolutionary defensive tactic: ordering his hoplites to kneel, plant their shields on the ground, and brace their spears, creating an impenetrable wall that repelled the Spartan charge. Beyond these successes, Chabrias also served as a mercenary commander for Acoris, Pharaoh of Egypt, from 389 to 385 BCE, defending Egypt against Persian aggression, and later aided Evagoras I of Cyprus, demonstrating his strategic acumen across diverse military contexts.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Chabrias's strategic innovations and decisive victory at Naxos in 376 BCE fundamentally shifted the balance of power in the Aegean, restoring Athenian naval supremacy and directly enabling the formation of the Second Athenian League. His tactics influenced subsequent Hellenistic warfare, demonstrating a lasting impact on military thought and practice.
